title: Variational Monte Carlo for the Hubbard model
abstract: In these lecture notes, we introduce the variational Monte Carlo method for the Hubbard model. First, we briefly introduce the single-orbital Hubbard model and its multi-orbital extension, focusing only on electronic models. Then, we introduce the general scheme under which variational Monte Carlo works and we present the variational wave functions that can properly describe superconductive and magnetic states in single-orbital and multi-orbital Hubbard models. We also detail how to perform Monte Carlo calculations for the given wave functions. We also describe how to optimize a variational wave function with the stochastic reconfiguration method. Finally, we present a few results for correlation functions that can be computed in variational Monte Carlo, to determine, for instance, the presence of charge or spin order and superconductivity.
summary: This lecture notes series introduces the Variational Monte Carlo method for studying the Hubbard model, covering both single- and multi-orbital extensions. It details the computational machinery, including the local estimator and Metropolis sampling, to calculate quantum expectation values. The work demonstrates how this technique can reveal complex correlated phenomena such as superconductivity and orbital selectivity in strongly interacting electron systems.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of studying correlated Hamiltonians, specifically the Hubbard model, in two dimensions where exact solutions are unavailable.
main_result: The Variational Monte Carlo method successfully computes quantum expectation values for the Hubbard model, allowing the diagnosis of phenomena like superconductivity and orbital selectivity.
method: It employs Variational Monte Carlo (VMC) sampling, utilizing a local estimator and the Metropolis algorithm to calculate averages over a variational wave function.
model_or_system: The primary model is the Hubbard Hamiltonian, presented in both single-orbital and multi-orbital extensions (including nearest/next-nearest neighbor hopping and various repulsion terms).
key_observables: Correlation functions (spin/charge order), electronic density per orbital ($n_\alpha$), and pairing correlations ($D_\alpha(r)$).
important_parameters: The interaction strength $U$, hopping parameters ($t, t'$), and filling factor ($n$).
main_assumptions: The method relies on constructing a variational Ansatz (e.g., Jastrow-Slater wave function) and assumes that the local estimator approach is tractable despite the complex Hilbert space.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate orbital-selective pairing correlations ($D_\alpha(r)$) and orbital occupation differentiation ($n_\alpha$) as a function of interaction strength $U$.
paper_structure: The notes suggest an introduction to the Hubbard model, followed by a detailed exposition of the VMC formalism (including local estimators and Metropolis sampling), and concluding with the application of the method to analyze specific correlated phenomena.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter, the VMC framework and the use of advanced wave function ansatze (like Jastrow factors) are general techniques for approximating ground states in complex quantum many-body systems, which has parallels in quantum simulation theory.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Upper left panel: Ground-state energy as a function of the range of backflow parameters on the 2D square lattice for t′/t = 0.4 and 0.75 at U/t = 8. A range equal to zero corresponds to no backflow correlations in the wave function. Lower left panel: Optimized backflow param- eters η|R−R′| as a function of the distance |R −R′| between lattice sites. Results for U/t = 3 and t′/t = 0.4 correspond to a metallic state, the others to Mott insulating states. Data are shown for a lattice with L = 98 sites [21]. Right panel: Energy (in units of 4t2 1/U), as a function of t1/U, for the 1D Hubbard model with t2/t1 = 1. Filled (empty) circles denote the results with (without) backflow...

Fig. 2: Results for 18 electrons on 18 sites as a function of U/t. Upper panels: Accuracy of energy ∆E = (E0 −Ev), Ev and E0 being the variational and the exact values, respectively. Lower panels: Overlap between the exact ground state and the variational wave functions. The variational state without backflow is denoted by blue triangles, the variational state with backflow correlations is denoted by red circles [20].

Fig. 3: Variational results for N(q) divided by |q|, as a function of |q|, for L = 98 (empty symbols) and for L = 162 (full symbols) at t′/t = 0.75. The metal-insulator transition takes place between U/t = 7 and U/t = 8, that is, where N(q) changes its behavior from linear to quadratic for |q| →0 [20].
Fig. 4: Spin-spin correlations S(q) at U/t1 = 12 for different values of the hopping ratio t2/t1. Arrows indicate the location of the peaks. Data are shown on a L = 120 lattice size [33].

Fig. 5: Square of the superconducting order parameter ϕ2 α in each orbital as a function of U at n = 3 + 1/3 [panel a)] and n = 3 + 2/3 [panel b)]. Data are for the L = 18 × 18 cluster. Square of the superconducting order parameter in the dxy [panel c)] and dxz [panel d)] orbitals as a function of n at U = 2eV (full squares) and at U = 0 (empty squares). Data are for the L = 12 × 12 cluster. All data are computed at J = 0.2U [25].
